name: Adept-2 (Adept automatic differentiation library)
baseline: ADOL-C and Ceres Solver autodiff (C++ operator-overloading AD tools); also finite differences
workload: Gradient of a Gaussian mixture model (10k data points, 30 to 53,600 parameters) and the bundle-adjustment Jacobian (reverse mode) in the ADBench AD-tool shootout.
claimed_speedup: Bundle adjustment Jacobian, smallest instance: Adept 6.79e-02 vs ADOL-C 8.50e-01 vs Ceres 2.26e-01 (about 12.5x and 3.3x faster, derived from page data); largest instance: Adept 6.63e+01 vs ADOL-C 7.09e+02 (about 10.7x, derived from page data); Ceres did not finish. GMM 10k points, 30 parameters: Adept (split) 2.86e-02 vs ADOL-C (split) 4.71e-01 (about 16x, derived from page data). Hand-written C++ derivative was still about 3.5x faster than Adept on BA (1.96e-02 vs 6.79e-02).
stars_or_usage: 189 stars; benchmark is the Microsoft ADBench suite (113 stars, archived July 2024)
tradeoffs: Reverse mode uses expression templates; the library also bundles array classes and optimisation routines. Apache-2.0 applies to the include/ and adept/ files per the README. Fixed-order first derivatives; no higher-order or vector-mode support as far as the ADBench text states.
caveats: The ADBench numbers come from a paper (Optimization Methods and Software 2018, shorter version at AD2016) whose tool versions date from the 2015-2016 era (the Adept of that time, not Adept-2); compiler and flags are not stated. On GMM without manual splitting ADOL-C was faster than Adept at medium sizes (3,300 parameters: ADOL-C 8.49e-01 vs Adept 9.76e-01; 10,700 parameters: 1.90 vs 3.11) and both tools failed on the largest instances. Ceres is forward-mode only in this test, which disadvantages it. Tapenade (C source transformation) was faster than Adept on GMM and BA. The paper does not restate the time unit in the table caption. Adept is not the incumbent in this category's baseline list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor).

name: OpenVINO (CPU inference runtime)
baseline: TensorFlow Lite with the XNNPACK delegate (XNNPACK)
workload: MobileNet V2 and ResNet 50 single-image inference latency/throughput on an 8-vCPU Google Cloud Ubuntu 16.04 VM, TFLite+XNNPACK vs OpenVINO.
claimed_speedup: ResNet 50: OpenVINO 62.55 ms vs TFLite+XNNPACK 118.3 ms (first table, thread count not labelled; about 1.9x, derived from page data); with 8 threads 16.70 ms vs 32.8 ms (about 2.0x, derived from page data). MobileNet V2 is a tie or a loss: 11.14 vs 11.48 ms (first table) and 3.56 vs 3.16 ms with 8 threads (XNNPACK faster). OpenVINO throughput-optimized mode reached 382.44 FPS vs 316.46 FPS for XNNPACK on MobileNet V2 with 8 threads.
hardware: Google Cloud VM, 8 vCPUs (CPU model not stated), Ubuntu 16.04 LTS
tradeoffs: Large toolkit (model converters, plugins for CPU/GPU/NPU) rather than a small kernel library; not a drop-in replacement for XNNPACK kernels inside TFLite.
caveats: The benchmark is a small personal repository (undated, Ubuntu 16.04 era) with unstated CPU model, compiler, flags and library versions, so it falls short of tier A; the XNNPACK and OpenVINO versions are old. OpenVINO wins on ResNet 50 but not on MobileNet V2 at 8 threads. A separate user report (XNNPACK issue 1803, Aug 2021, EC2 T2.Large, MobileNet V1 and AlexNet) says OpenVINO took 50% of XNNPACK's latency, but it got no maintainer reply and is anecdotal.

name: Nervana neon (GPU convolution kernels)
baseline: cuDNN R4 (fp16 and fp32, via Torch bindings)
workload: Full forward+backward pass time (ms) of AlexNet, Overfeat-fast, OxfordNet (VGG model A) and GoogleNet V1 convolution stacks on a Titan X in the convnet-benchmarks shootout.
claimed_speedup: OxfordNet model A fp32: neon 320 ms vs cuDNN R4 529 ms (about 1.65x, derived from page data); fp16: 254 vs 471 ms. GoogleNet V1 fp32: 270 vs 470 ms; fp16: 230 vs 462 ms. Overfeat fp32: 211 vs 268 ms; fp16: 176 vs 242 ms. cuDNN R4 won AlexNet: fp16 71 vs 78 ms, fp32 81 vs 87 ms.
hardware: 6-core Intel Core i7-5930K @ 3.50GHz + NVIDIA Titan X, Ubuntu 14.04 x86_64
tradeoffs: Python framework with custom GPU kernels; not callable as a C++ library. Intel discontinued the project, so there is no support for newer GPUs or cuDNN versions.
caveats: Numbers are from 2016 and compare against cuDNN R4 only; later cuDNN releases added Winograd and other algorithms, so today's gap is likely smaller or reversed (not measured here). The suite states CPU and GPU but no compiler or flags. neon's README itself claims '2x speed of cuDNNv4'. The suite's Nervana rows link to convnet-benchmarks/nervana/README.md, which was not opened, so it is not confirmed on the page that the benchmarked kernels are exactly the code in the neon repository.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): soumith/convnet-benchmarks README (found via the query 'github CUDA kernels "faster than cuDNN" convolution OR attention OR layernorm benchmark open source C++')

name: CTranslate2
baseline: PyTorch (OpenNMT-py, Hugging Face Transformers), TensorFlow (OpenNMT-tf), Marian and FasterTransformer
workload: Tokens generated per second translating the English-German newstest2014 set with Transformer base models on CPU (4 threads) and GPU.
claimed_speedup: CPU (4 threads): OpenNMT-py/PyTorch 275.8 tok/s vs CTranslate2 658.8 (fp32) and 1126.2 (int8 + vocabulary map); Marian 344.5 vs CTranslate2 525.0 (696.1 int8) on the OPUS-MT model. GPU (A10G): PyTorch 1795.2 vs CTranslate2 6634.7 (fp32) and 10990.7 (float16); FasterTransformer float16 8592.5 vs CTranslate2 float16 10990.7.
hardware: CPU: AWS c5.2xlarge, Intel Xeon Platinum 8275CL, 4 threads; GPU: AWS g5.xlarge, NVIDIA A10G, CUDA 11 (driver 510.47.03)
tradeoffs: Inference only, for Transformer model families via converters; adds quantization (int8/int16/fp16). Its CPU backends include Intel MKL, oneDNN and Ruy, and GPU uses CUDA libraries, so it builds on rather than replaces the incumbent kernels.
caveats: First-party README numbers (CTranslate2 3.6.0 against PyTorch 1.13.1 and TensorFlow 2.11.0, i.e. older library versions) with public benchmark scripts in tools/benchmark, but no compiler or flags and prebuilt packages; baselines are whole frameworks, not oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK or Eigen kernels, so this does not show a kernel-level win over them. FasterTransformer fp32 was faster than CTranslate2 fp32 on the GPU (6979.0 vs 6634.7 tok/s). The README itself warns relative performance changes with settings.

name: TTV (tlib tensor-times-vector library)
baseline: Eigen Tensor (sequential in-place tensor-times-vector); also TBLIS and TCL
workload: Mode-q tensor-times-vector products for symmetric (order 2-7, 324 cases) and asymmetric (order 2-10, 1296 cases) shapes in single and double precision.
claimed_speedup: README plots (read from the single-precision speedup figures, approximate): TTV over Eigen is mostly about 3x to 15x with outliers into the hundreds (asymmetric cases reach several hundred x); over TBLIS typically about 3x to 5x; over TCL mostly 1x to 10x with some cases below 1x. README text: for large tensors it 'reaches peak matrix-times-vector performance'. (plot readings are derived from page data)
hardware: Intel Core i9-7900X (10 cores, 20 threads, 3.3 GHz)
tradeoffs: Covers only the tensor-times-vector contraction (loops-over-GEMV/DOT), not general contractions; needs contiguous storage; relies on a BLAS (OpenBLAS, MKL or BLIS) for peak speed.
caveats: Results are shown only as plots in the README (no tables); the benchmark driver that produced them is not in the repository's test directory (only unit tests), so it cannot be rerun from the repo. The comparison uses old library versions (Eigen 3.3.90, TBLIS 1.0.0, TCL 0.1.1). Eigen is run sequentially, so parallel speedup inflates the ratio. The README badge says GPL while the GitHub licence field says LGPL-3.0. A peer-reviewed ICCS 2019 paper by the same author is cited but was not opened.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page 'tensor-contraction' listing ttv, then the README Experiments section

name: FeatherCNN
baseline: Caffe2 with Eigen, Caffe with OpenBLAS, NNPACK Winograd and TensorFlow Lite (ARM CPUs)
workload: End-to-end CNN inference time (VGG-16, GoogleNet, ResNet-50, MobileNet V1, SqueezeNet, DenseNet-121) on six ARM devices, plus a VGG-16 per-layer GFLOPS comparison against NNPACK.
claimed_speedup: Huawei D05 (64 Cortex-A72 cores), best thread count: speedup over Caffe2+Eigen 12.84x on VGG-16 and 4.45x on GoogleNet; over Caffe+OpenBLAS 10.86x on VGG-16 and 13.7x on GoogleNet (wiki's FeatherCNN Speedup column). VGG-16 on iPhone 7, 2 cores: FeatherCNN 284 ms vs TensorFlow Lite 905 ms (about 3.2x, derived from page data; the wiki does not label TFLite's thread count).
hardware: Samsung S8 (Snapdragon 835), iPhone 7 (A10), Huawei D05 (Hi1616, 64 cores), Phytium FT1500A/16, RK3399, Raspberry Pi 3B
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars; developed by Tencent for a mobile game
tradeoffs: Converts Caffe models only; ARM CPU focused; no third-party dependencies and a small library size.
caveats: First-party wiki numbers from late 2017, which the page itself says may have changed; compiler and flags are not stated. The README badge and GitHub page say BSD-3-Clause but no LICENSE file was found at the master branch (raw URL returned 404), so usability is marked reference until verified. Baselines are Caffe2+Eigen (Eigen-based convolution, not Eigen Tensor itself), TFLite as tested in late 2017, and NNPACK.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page 'inference-engine' (C++) listing FeatherCNN, then its wiki Benchmarks page

name: ByteTransformer
baseline: PyTorch, TensorFlow, NVIDIA FasterTransformer and DeepSpeed BERT inference
workload: Standard BERT encoder execution time (ms) on an A100 at batch 1 and batch 16, sequence lengths 64 to 1024, average length 0.6 of maximum.
claimed_speedup: Batch 16, sequence 1024: ByteTransformer 24.70 ms vs PyTorch 53.21, FasterTransformer 50.28, FasterTransformer with remove-padding 45.22, DeepSpeed 59.96 ms (about 1.8x vs the best baseline, derived from page data). Batch 1, sequence 1024: 3.16 ms vs PyTorch 4.2, FasterTransformer 4.51 ms.
hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPU (variant and host CPU not stated); CUDA 11.6
tradeoffs: BERT-like encoders only, NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 7.0 to 8.0; padding-free algorithm targets variable-length batches; Python and C++ APIs plus a PyTorch plugin.
caveats: First-party README numbers (the benchmark script benchmark/bert_bench.sh is public, but compiler flags and CPU are not stated); an IEEE IPDPS 2023 paper (arXiv 2210.03052) is cited but was not opened. At short sequences ByteTransformer is not always fastest: batch 1 seq 192-384 FasterTransformer is slightly ahead (1.26 vs 1.36 ms at 192), and batch 16 seq 64 FasterTransformer with remove-padding wins (1.93 vs 2.09 ms). Baselines are frameworks and FasterTransformer, not cuDNN, so it is not shown to beat cuDNN kernels directly.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub README search for transformer inference kernels (ByteDance repos checked via raw README after the query 'github CUDA kernels "faster than cuDNN" ...')

name: LightSeq
baseline: PyTorch fp16 and PyTorch QAT (Transformer and BERT training and inference)
workload: Training speedup on one A100 and inference speedup on eight A100s for Transformer and BERT models, relative to PyTorch fp16 mixed precision.
claimed_speedup: Up to 3x faster fp16 training vs PyTorch fp16; up to 5x faster int8 training vs PyTorch QAT; inference up to 12x (fp16) and 15x (int8) vs PyTorch fp16. README tables: Transformer inference batch 32, seq 8: 11.82x (fp16), 14.44x (int8); BERT inference batch 32, seq 128: only 1.82x (fp16).
hardware: NVIDIA A100 (1 for training, 8 for inference); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Built on cuBLAS, Thrust and CUB plus fused custom kernels; Python wheels support only Python 3.6-3.8 on Linux; archived read-only.
caveats: First-party README speedups with no raw timings, no compiler/flags and no public benchmark script identified in the README; the PyTorch baseline is eager fp16 rather than a tuned cuDNN or FasterTransformer path, which inflates the headline ratios (BERT inference at batch 32, seq 128 is only 1.82x). The README's headline 'up to 15x' is slightly above the largest table entry (14.44x).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub README search for transformer inference kernels (ByteDance repos checked via raw README)

name: Decoding Attention (Bruce-Lee-LY)
baseline: Flash-Decoding (FlashAttention v2.6.3) and FlashInfer v0.1.6 decode attention
workload: Decode-stage multi-head attention (32 heads, head dim 128, FP16) on an RTX 3090, sweeping sequence length and batch size; MLA on an H20 is also plotted.
claimed_speedup: README text: better than Flash-Decoding and FlashInfer when sequence length is below 1536 (FlashInfer and Flash-Decoding win above 1536), and 'regardless of batch size' better than both at sequence length 128. Reading the batch-size plot by eye (approximate, derived from page data): about 1.5x Flash-Decoding and about 1.0x FlashInfer at batch sizes of 128 and above.
tradeoffs: Uses CUDA cores, not tensor cores; decode stage only; MHA, MQA, GQA and MLA with FP16/BF16; C++ and Python APIs.
caveats: Single-developer repository whose results are plots with no numeric tables (y-axis labelled only 0 and 1); no compiler flags; the repository has two commits. Baselines are FlashAttention-family kernels, not cuDNN. The README concedes the baselines are faster at long sequences.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page 'flash-attention' (C++) listing decoding_attention

name: NNPACK (Winograd/FFT convolution)
workload: Two large 3x3 convolutions (256 input / 128 output channels at 128x128; 192 input / 96 output channels at 256x256) on a 6-core 4.3 GHz x86 CPU, XNNPACK convolution_bench vs NNPACK benchmark_conv with the 8x8 Winograd algorithm.
claimed_speedup: NNPACK 31.95 ms and 76.17 ms (91.4 and 89.3 GFLOPS) vs XNNPACK 1345.8 ms and 3060.0 ms (about 7.07 and 7.05 GFLOPS): roughly 42x and 40x lower time (derived from page data); the reporter says 3-5x slower on their real networks on arm64 and x86.
hardware: 6-core CPU at 4300 MHz, caches L1/L2/L3 32 KiB/256 KiB/9216 KiB (model not named), Ubuntu
stars_or_usage: 1.7k stars; backend in PyTorch mobile, Caffe2, MXNet, TVM
tradeoffs: Convolution-focused (Winograd for 3x3 stride-1, FFT up to 16x16, implicit GEMM), floating point only; GFLOPS are 'effective' because Winograd does fewer multiplies than direct convolution.
caveats: Evidence is one user's GitHub issue (June 2020, user Kepnu4) with the CPU model, compiler and flags not stated; the roughly 7 GFLOPS XNNPACK result looks low for the stated CPU, so it may not reflect XNNPACK's best path (unverified), and the issue was closed with no maintainer explanation visible. Effective GFLOPS compare different algorithms. The GitHub repository is no longer maintained (last commit February 2023).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): query 'github "faster than XNNPACK" OR "outperforms XNNPACK" CPU inference kernels benchmark' surfaced XNNPACK issues; issue 689 compares XNNPACK with NNPACK

name: HyperJet (hyper-dual number automatic differentiation)
workload: Value, gradient and dense Hessian of a cable strain-energy sum (n = 3, 6, 12, 24 variables), median ns per evaluation over 7 repetitions with Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Second order, static size: HyperJet 101 ns vs Eigen AutoDiffScalar nested 328 ns and autodiff dual2nd 375 ns at n=6 (3.3x vs the faster of the two); 921 vs 2888 and 2425 ns at n=12 (2.6x); 12,214 vs 22,105 and 17,679 ns at n=24 (1.5x); 15 vs 18 and 127 ns at n=3 (1.2x). First order (gradient only) there is no winner: HyperJet 244 ns vs AutoDiffScalar 245 ns vs ceres::Jet 304 ns at n=24.
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG (Release CMake build; benchmark verifies identical values, gradients and Hessians before timing)
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, macOS 26.5; Eigen 3.4.0, autodiff v1.1.2, Ceres 2.2.0
tradeoffs: Header-only C++23 (Python bindings via pybind11); the fast variant needs the variable count at compile time, while the dynamic-size variant is 1.9x to 43x slower than the static one in the README's own text and, in its second-order table, is slower than both Eigen AutoDiffScalar and autodiff dual2nd at every size tested (n=3 to 24).
caveats: Author-run benchmark (first-party) on a single Apple Silicon machine, but the benchmark code is in the repository and the README is candid that there is no gain for gradient-only work. The Eigen baseline is AutoDiffScalar from Eigen's unsupported module, not Eigen Tensor. The README notes inlining decisions change absolute times by about 1.6x and that the benchmark forces inlining uniformly. Small project (17 stars).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page 'autodiff' (C++, sorted by stars) listing oberbichler/HyperJet, then its README Performance section

name: Marlin (FP16xINT4 LLM matmul kernel)
baseline: FP16 PyTorch matmul (calls CUTLASS) and other 4-bit kernels: torch-nightly, exllamav2, AWQ, bitsandbytes
workload: 16-bit x 4-bit (group size 128) matrix multiplication on a 72k x 18k weight matrix on an NVIDIA A10 across batch sizes 1-128, plus the linear layers of Llama and Falcon models at batch size 16 on A10, 3090, A6000 and A100.
claimed_speedup: Plot of speedup over FP16 PyTorch on the A10 (values read from the README plot, approximate, derived from page data): Marlin about 3.9x at batch sizes 1 to 16 and 3.8x at 32, about 3.1x at 64 and 1.55x at 128; at batch 16 torch-nightly about 1.4x, exllamav2 about 0.7x, AWQ about 0.3x, bitsandbytes about 0.4x. Model layers at batch 16: roughly 3.4x to 4.25x on A10, 3090 and A6000, and about 2.2x to 3.6x on A100. README text: 'close to ideal (4x)' up to batch sizes of 16-32.
hardware: NVIDIA A10 (peak plot); A10, RTX 3090, A6000 and A100 (model layers); CUDA >= 11.8, torch >= 2.0
tradeoffs: Weight-only FP16xINT4 inference kernel for Ampere/Ada GPUs (compute capability >= 8.0); the README says it is not yet optimised for Hopper; needs quantised, reshuffled weights; PyTorch extension.
caveats: First-party README results shown only as plots (no tables; compiler flags and host not stated); an arXiv paper (2408.11743) is cited but is a preprint and was not opened. The baseline is FP16 PyTorch matmul, which the plot labels as calling CUTLASS, not cuDNN or cuBLAS directly, and the headline compares 4-bit weights to 16-bit weights, so part of the speedup is the memory-traffic saving of quantisation rather than a faster FP16 kernel. Speedups fall off above batch size 32 (1.55x at 128) and are lower on A100.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub README search for GPU kernels that beat the incumbent (Marlin README plots peak.png and models.png)

name: FasterTransformer
baseline: TensorFlow XLA (FP16) and PyTorch TorchScript (FP16) transformer encoder and decoder inference
workload: BERT-base encoder and Transformer decoder/decoding end-to-end translation on a T4, speedup relative to TensorFlow XLA and PyTorch TorchScript under FP16, using the repo's benchmark scripts.
claimed_speedup: BERT base on T4 vs TensorFlow XLA FP16: about 3x for small batch/sequence, about 5x for large batch/sequence using Effective FasterTransformer with INT8-v2; vs PyTorch TorchScript: 4x to 6x small, about 5x large. Decoding vs TensorFlow: FT-Decoder 1.5x to 3x, FT-Decoding 4x to 18x; vs PyTorch: FT-Decoder 1.2x to 3x, FT-Decoding 3.8x to 13x.
hardware: NVIDIA T4 (mclk 5000 MHz, pclk 1590 MHz) with Intel Xeon E5-2670 @ 2.60GHz; also 8xA100-80GB with AMD EPYC 7742
tradeoffs: Built on CUDA, cuBLAS and cuBLASLt with TensorFlow, PyTorch and Triton backends; the repository notes development moved to TensorRT-LLM, so it receives no new features.
caveats: First-party NVIDIA README numbers shown as figures (speedup ranges are quoted in text); benchmark scripts are in the repo (benchmarks/bert/*.sh, benchmarks/decoding/*.sh) but compiler and flags are not stated. Baselines are framework implementations of the era (TensorFlow XLA, TorchScript), not cuDNN. Third-party tables (ByteTransformer README, CTranslate2 README) show FasterTransformer is beaten by newer kernels in several settings.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub README search for GPU transformer inference kernels (FasterTransformer README performance section; baseline for the ByteTransformer and CTranslate2 tables)
